data.title: Loyalist Announces $1,001,000 Non-Brokered Private Placement
data.description:
(TheNewswire)

Toronto, Ontario – TheNewswire – November 20, 2026 – Loyalist Exploration Limited (“Loyalist” or the “Company”) is pleased to announce a non-brokered private placement consisting of the sale of up to 28,600,000 common shares in the capital of the Company to be issued as “flow-through shares” within the meaning of subsection 66(15) of the Income Tax Act (Canada) (“FT Shares”) at a price of $0.035 per FT Share for gross proceeds of up to $1,001,000 (the “Offering”). The FT Shares will be offered to purchasers in all provinces of Canada pursuant to the “accredited investor” and “minimum amount investment” exemptions under National Instrument 45-106 - Prospectus Exemptions.

The gross proceeds from the sale of the FT Shares will be used to incur eligible “Canadian exploration expenses” that qualify as “flow-through mining expenditures”, as such terms are defined in the Income Tax Act (Canada), on the Company’s Timmins-area projects, which will be renounced to the subscribers of FT Shares with an effective date no later than December 31, 2026.

The Company may pay finder’s fees to eligible finders in connection with the Offering.

All of the securities that will be issued in connection with the Offering will be subject to a hold period expiring four months and one day after the date of issuance. Completion of the Offering is subject to the receipt of all required regulatory approvals, including the approval of the Canadian Securities Exchange.

The securities offered have not been registered under the United States Securities Act of 1933, as amended, and may not be offered or sold in the United States or to, or for the account or benefit of, U.S. persons absent registration or an applicable exemption from registration requirements. This release does not constitute an offer for sale of securities in the United States.

It is anticipated that the first closing of the Offering will occur on or about December 11, 2026.

Neither the Canadian Securities Exchange nor its Market Regulator (as that term is defined in the policies of the Canadian Securities Exchange) have reviewed or accept responsibility for the adequacy or accuracy of this release.

About Loyalist Exploration Limited

Loyalist is a Canadian mineral exploration and development company focused on creating long-term shareholder value through the advancement of high-quality mineral projects in Timmins, Ontario.

The Company's flagship 100%-owned Tully Gold Project, located in the prolific Timmins Gold Camp of northeastern Ontario, is a growing underground gold project with significant exploration upside and excellent development potential. Supported by a high-confidence Indicated and Inferred Mineral Resource Estimate, favourable infrastructure, and a modern geological model, Tully provides a strong platform for continued development and expansion.

Loyalist's strategy is to systematically advance the Tully Gold Project to production while growing the deposit and continuing to evaluate opportunities to expand its portfolio of high-quality mineral assets.

The Company also looks forward to advancing exploration activities on its three other Timmins based projects – DeSantis, Gold Rush and Loveland.

The Company is committed to maintaining the highest standards of technical excellence and responsible development throughout all stages of project advancement.

For further information please visit the Company's website at www.loyalistexploration.com or contact:

Loyalist Exploration Limited

Errol Farr, President and CEO

Email: efarr@loyalistexploration.com

Tel: 647-296-1270

data.title: Garuda Indonesia to Offer More Choice, Flexibility and Value With New Ticket Options in 2027
data.description:
JAKARTA, Nov 20, 2026 - (ACN Newswire) - Garuda Indonesia is set to launch a wider range of ticket options in the first quarter of 2027, giving travellers more choice, greater flexibility and competitive price points tailored to their individual travel needs. The new offering marks a key milestone in the airline's customer-focused transformation, making its full-service experience more accessible to a broader range of travellers.

Under the new structure, passengers will be able to choose from several ticket products, each offering a different combination of benefits, including baggage allowance, seat selection, flexibility to change travel plans and other travel privileges.

For domestic Economy Class, the new products will include Standard, Smart and Flex, while international Economy Class will offer an additional Saver option. Business Class passengers will have a choice of Business and Business Flex.

Each category is designed to accommodate different travel priorities, allowing passengers to choose the combination of benefits and flexibility that best suits their needs and preferences.

The new offering will also make it easier for customers to compare ticket options and understand what is included before making a booking. Previously, certain fare choices were dependent on booking-class availability, particularly during peak travel periods. Under the new structure, Garuda Indonesia aims to make its ticket categories more consistently available, giving travellers clearer choices across different price points.

Garuda Indonesia Director of Transformation Neil Raymond Mills said the initiative reflects the airline's commitment to making its ongoing transformation more meaningful to customers, beyond improvements to its business fundamentals.

"Every journey is different, and so are our customers' priorities. Some value greater flexibility, while others are looking for the right combination of services at a competitive price point. By recognising these differences, we can make the Garuda Indonesia experience more relevant and accessible to a wider range of travellers, while maintaining the distinctive service that defines our airline," Neil said.

The expanded ticket offering is scheduled to launch in the first quarter of 2027, with the new product structure developed in accordance with the prevailing aviation regulatory framework.

The initiative is also expected to strengthen the airline's competitiveness while contributing to a healthier and more sustainable aviation industry.

"For us, the success of this initiative goes beyond introducing new ticket products. It is about ensuring that customers have a clear understanding of what they are choosing and can enjoy a seamless experience across every touchpoint, from booking to boarding. This is an important part of how we are translating our transformation into tangible improvements in the way we serve our customers," Neil concluded.

For more information, please visit: https://www.garuda-indonesia.com/id/en/garuda-indonesia-experience/on-ground/fare-choices

corpcomm@garuda-indonesia.com

data.title: Gold slides toward worst week in eight months on hawkish Fed outlook
data.description:
Key points:
  • Gold slips for fifth session, hits lowest since September 2025
  • Silver, platinum and palladium head for second weekly decline
  • Fed's Paulson says Fed will need to raise rates again
  • Physical gold demand in India and China picked up this week

By Sherin Sans

Gold extended its sharp selloff on Friday, hovering near a more than one-year low and heading for its steepest weekly decline in eight months, as expectations of a hawkish Federal Reserve boosted the dollar and Treasury yields.

Spot gold fell 1% to $3,585.92 per ounce by 1113 GMT, after touching its lowest level since September 4, 2025 at $3,513.54 earlier in the session. Bullion has shed about 8% so far this week, the most since the week ended March 20.

US gold futures for December delivery dropped 2.7% to $3,587.90 per ounce.

"Gold is under renewed pressure from hawkish Fed expectations, which are lifting real yields and the US dollar and raising the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset. The ongoing AI-related equity selloff is also prompting some forced liquidations of gold positions to cover losses elsewhere," Critical Metals CEO Tony Sage said.

Asian shares tumbled on Friday and were headed for their worst week since 2020 after Anthropic's debut failed to restore investor confidence in the AI sector, while the dollar extended its rally on safe-haven demand.

The selloff in gold gathered pace after Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson joined other policymakers in flagging inflation risks that could warrant another interest-rate increase, reinforcing expectations that US borrowing costs will rise further.

Markets see a 99% chance of a 25-basis-point US rate hike in December, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

Meanwhile, physical gold demand in India and China strengthened this week as the price slump attracted bargain hunters, with investors in China viewing the correction as a buying opportunity.

Among other metals, spot silver fell 0.4% to $42.58 per ounce, platinum dropped 2.6% to $1,309.36 and palladium slid 0.3% to $906.67.

All three metals are poised for second straight weekly declines.

"Silver, platinum and palladium are declining in tandem with gold primarily because of the same macro drivers. Silver is typically more volatile and has amplified the move this week. Platinum and palladium are also sensitive to growth concerns that accompany tighter monetary policy," Sage said.

data.title: Weekend Reads: 'Made with Europe,' Russia's war chest and US measles crisis
data.description:
By Anna Szymanski

Looking for inspiration? Every Friday, Weekend Reads rounds up what the Reuters Open Interest team has been reading, watching and listening to.

This week's picks span Europe's trade rethink, Russia's energy billions, America's measles crisis, and more.

This weekend, we're reading...

MIKE DOLAN, ROI Finance & Markets Columnist: This piece from Brussels-based think tank Bruegel argues that the European Union should shift its "Made in Europe" procurement initiative to a "Made with Europe" one — something British Prime Minister Andy Burnham might want to read ahead of Friday's EU-UK summit.

ANDY HOME, ROI Metals Columnist: The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies examines whether China has upheld its commitment to loosen rare earth export controls. It all depends on the export destination.

GAVIN MAGUIRE, ROI Global Energy Transition Columnist: New analysis from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air shows Russia's fossil fuel export earnings hit their highest level since late 2022 in October. As Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met this week, Russia's energy revenues were in focus as a potential bargaining chip in broader geopolitical negotiations.

The data suggests Russia entered the discussions from a position of relative financial strength, with resilient fossil-fuel export earnings continuing to bankroll the economy despite years of sanctions and trade restrictions.

CLYDE RUSSELL, ROI Asia Commodities and Energy Columnist: The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook examines the long-term ramifications of the Middle East crisis, suggesting that more countries could pursue energy independence.

ANNA SZYMANSKI, ROI Editor-in-Charge: The US has lost its hard-won measles-free status under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. This sobering Reuters special report found that preschool vaccination rates have fallen sharply since he was appointed.

We're listening to...

RON BOUSSO, ROI Energy Columnist: This episode of the Energy Unplugged podcast examines how the war in Iran has reshaped the LNG market — and why it still faces the prospect of a major supply glut.

And we're watching...

ANNA SZYMANSKI, ROI Editor-in-Charge: Check out the new, expanded version of the Reuters Morning Bid podcast, hosted by my ROI colleague Mike Dolan and a set of Reuters journalists, including yours truly. In the new format, we feature interviews with industry leaders and experts as well as deep dives into a wide range of topics from the AI metals push to the "GTA flu." data.title: Euro zone bond yields drop as investors seek safety from AI-trade rout
data.description:
Euro zone bond yields extended their falls on Friday as global stocks slid on doubts about the AI trade, sending investors towards safe-haven government debt.

Anthropic shares jumped in the company's blockbuster IPO on Thursday but did not revive excitement around the broader AI trade, with US futures and European shares dropping and Asian equities (.MISX00000PUS) set for their worst week since March.

That benefited safe-haven German bonds, the euro area benchmark, sending 10-year yields down 9 basis points to 3.322% (DE10YT=RR).

Two-year yields, which are more sensitive to central bank rate expectations, also fell 9 bps to 3.071% (DE2YT=RR). Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Still, the move in euro zone bonds was not particularly large considering the broader market risk-off, said Lyn Graham-Taylor, a senior rates strategist at Rabobank.

"It's quite a decent move in bond yields, but you could argue that it's not particularly massive for some of the equity declines we've seen," he said.

French and Italian bonds (FR10YT=RR), also picked up, with yields down around 7 bps.

Europe's benchmark STOXX 600 index pared losses and was last down 1.1%, on track for a 5% weekly drop.

Euro zone bond yields have fallen from multiyear or multidecade highs in September and October as energy prices have cooled and tech stocks have dropped.

It was too soon to say whether the AI selloff would bring an extended period of strength for bonds, Graham-Taylor said, as markets were also watching oil prices and the economy.

Oil prices fell on Friday, also boosting bonds, with Brent crude futures dropping 2% to $90 a barrel, down sharply from $118 a barrel in late October.

On the macro front, the European Commission will release flash data on November's consumer confidence later on Friday.

Earlier in the day, ECB President Christine Lagarde said the European Central Bank will make its currency swap lines with other countries more accessible to shield the euro area from outside financial shocks and boost the euro's global role.

About Quantum Base

Quantum Base is a quantum science company setting a new global standard in authentication. It helps to stop counterfeiting and global illicit trade with its patented Q-ID® smartphone authentication. Q-ID® is a physical fingerprint created by atomic-scale variations in quantum-active ink, readable by smartphone in under three seconds,

Each Q-ID® is checked against the atomically secure fingerprint captured when it was printed. Q-ID® is printed on standard litho or flexo presses, so security printers can add it to existing print lines. It is authenticated with existing, unmodified smartphones. Q-ID® entered large-volume commercial use in 2024. More than two billion Q-ID®s now protect products worldwide, backed by 40+ patents and independent adversarial testing. Security printers and government revenue agencies use Q-ID® around the world.

The Group also develops Q-RAND®, a nanoscale, true quantum random number generator that complies with the NIST randomness test suite.

data.title: TD Cowen Names UnitedHealth Its 2027 Best Idea —  Why Analyst Sees Mid-To-High-Teens EPS Growth For UNH Stock
data.description:
Key points:
  • The firm sees a path toward mid-to-high-teens EPS growth through at least 2028, supported by Medicare Advantage benefit design, Optum Health recovery and improving Commercial and Medicaid margins, investing.com reported.
  • Earlier this week, Mizuho described the proposed CMS rule as an incremental negative for Medicare Advantage margins, adding that United Health and Humana will be most affected.
  • Twenty-two of 26 analysts covering the stock rate it ‘Buy’ or ‘Strong Buy,’ while four rate the stock ‘Hold,’ according to Koyfin.

UnitedHealth Group Inc (UNH) was upgraded to ‘Buy’ from ‘Hold’ by TD Cowen on Friday, with the firm naming the healthcare company its 2027 ‘Best Idea.’

According to TheFly, TD Cowen also raised its price target to $455 from $402, implying approximately 37.7% upside potential from the stock’s last close.

UNH shares traded 1.4% higher in premarket trading at the time of writing, after three consecutive sessions of losses following the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) proposal for tighter Medicare Advantage oversight on Monday.

Earlier this week, Mizuho analyst Ann Hynes described the proposed CMS rule as an incremental negative for Medicare Advantage margins, citing increased audit scrutiny as a potential headwind for insurers, according to TheFly. The firm expects UnitedHealth and Humana to be the most affected due to their exposure to Medicare Advantage, followed by CVS Health, Elevance Health, Centene and Molina Healthcare.

TD Cowen Sees Earnings Growth Across Key Business Segments

The firm expects UnitedHealth to deliver mid-to-high-teens earnings-per-share (EPS) growth through at least 2028, supported by its Medicare Advantage benefit design, an expected recovery at Optum Health, and improving Commercial and Medicaid performance, according to a report published by Investing.com.

TD Cowen said 2027 Medicare Advantage benefits appear rational and that a multi-year improvement cycle at Optum Health remains on track. It also sees room for earnings growth as Commercial and Medicaid margins improve, adding that both remain well below target levels.

The firm raised its 2027 and 2028 earnings estimates but said its forecasts do not account for full normalization across Optum Health, Commercial and Medicaid. Meanwhile, the firm sees approximately $2 per share in additional embedded earnings opportunities from these segments that are not yet reflected in its estimates.

Twenty-two of 26 analysts covering the stock rate it ‘Buy’ or ‘Strong Buy,’ while four rate it ‘Hold,’ according to Koyfin. Their 12-month price targets range from $380 to $531, with an average of $476.16.

How Retail Views UNH

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits remained ‘extremely bullish’ over the past 24 hours, amid ‘extremely high’ message volumes.

UNH shares traded marginally higher year-to-date.

data.title: Gold, Silver Drop to Lowest Levels in Over a Year — Update
data.description:
By Megan Cheah and Farhan Rafid

Gold and silver fell to their lowest levels in over a year on Friday as expectations of higher interest rates globally and a broader selloff across commodities pressured precious metals.

Expectations for tighter monetary policy appear to have overshadowed the typical demand for gold as a safe haven for risk-averse investors. The precious metals weakened despite heavy losses across Asian stock markets.

December gold futures fell 3% to $3,573.60 a troy ounce, while spot silver declined around 0.8% to $42.42 an ounce.

The decline in precious metals is part of a broader selloff across commodities, with investors cutting exposure, unwinding crowded positions and taking profits ahead of year-end, according to Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank.

Hansen said in a note Friday that precious metals had suffered the largest losses, with silver falling 14% and gold nearly 8% this week. Rising borrowing costs, a stronger U.S. dollar and concerns about artificial-intelligence investment have added to selling pressure, while losses in other assets have increased demand for cash.

Gold's failure to attract safe-haven demand during the equity-market selloff suggests investors are selling liquid assets to cover losses and reduce risk, Hansen said. However, holdings in gold exchange-traded funds have remained broadly unchanged over the past month despite the decline in prices, indicating longer-term investors have largely maintained their exposure.

The gold-to-silver ratio climbed to 85.58 Friday, about 25% above its average over nearly three decades. The ratio measures how many ounces of silver are needed to buy an ounce of gold, with a higher reading indicating silver is relatively cheaper.

Carsten Menke, head of Next Generation Research at Julius Baer, said silver's decline below $45 an ounce, alongside a gold-to-silver ratio above 85, could present a buying opportunity. However, the bank is waiting for signs that prices have bottomed before turning more positive, as further declines remain possible. Julius Baer maintains a neutral view on silver and a constructive outlook for gold.

Copper also declined, with December futures falling 1.6% to $5.5460 a pound. The industrial metal is on track to lose around 9% this week, reaching an eight-month low amid concerns about global growth, Chinese demand and the outlook for artificial-intelligence infrastructure investment, according to Saxo Bank.

Julius Baer upgraded its outlook for copper to constructive following the recent correction, saying the metal remains at risk of a structural supply deficit as demand from electric vehicles, clean energy and battery storage increases. Copper prices have fallen more than 15% from their highs this year, but the bank expects electrification-related technologies to account for around 30% of demand by 2035, compared with 25% in 2025. Menke said mining investments are increasing but might come too late to prevent a shortage.

Japan's consumer inflation data for October released Friday showed prices were accelerating past the Bank of Japan's target. That reinforced expectations for tighter policy as policymakers grew increasingly worried about the risk of higher prices due to increased energy costs, persistent yen weakness and rising semiconductor prices amid the artificial-intelligence boom.

"A rate hike at the next meeting in December looks highly likely, and the central bank will likely discuss an additional increase in March 2027, when inflation is expected to accelerate into the 3% range," said Takeshi Minami, an economist at Norinchukin Research Institute.

Minutes from the U.S. Federal Reserve's October meeting released Wednesday also showed that nearly all policymakers expected higher interest rates would be needed to lower inflation.

The minutes "showed strong alignment from Fed officials on the need for additional rate hikes," said MUFG analysts. Markets recently priced in a 93% probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike next month.

Many also expect the European Central Bank to raise rates in December after staying on hold last month, as it is under pressure to address the inflationary backdrop given persistently high energy prices.

A higher interest-rate environment typically diminishes the allure of nonyielding assets such as gold and silver. The hawkish Fed view also likely lifted the dollar, which makes gold and silver, both dollar-denominated commodities, more expensive for investors holding other currencies.

Upcoming U.S. economic data could shape expectations for the size of a December interest-rate move by the Fed, said Critical Metals' Tony Sage in a note. This includes the second estimate for the country's third-quarter gross domestic product growth due next week.

"Firm readings could lift yields further and extend gold's losses, while softer prints may offer some relief," he added.

Write to Megan Cheah at megan.cheah@wsj.com and to Farhan Rahid at farhan.rafid@wsj.com

"I don't expect that to change unless they bring the war to the end." By temporarily lifting the sanctions, the U.S. has given Russia a little window to show how ending the conflict could boost export revenues for diesel, he said. (adam.whittaker@wsj.com)

data.title: AI’s last stand?
data.description:
By Anna Szymanski

From the Editor

This should have been a fantastic week for AI bulls: Nvidia’s earnings were stellar, and Anthropic stormed the public markets with a blockbuster $81 billion IPO. But global equities have had a tough few days, with Asian stocks recording their worst week since 2020. The fallout from the Jensen Huang scandal continued with tighter US curbs on chip sales to China and news of more investigations, while fears of aggressive Federal Reserve rate hikes also rattled investors.

Perhaps the hype surrounding the Anthropic IPO should be seen as a warning sign that the four-year-old bull market is getting stretched.

Anthropic’s IPO was the one thing – besides perhaps the long-awaited release of Grand Theft Auto VI – that could kick Nvidia out of the spotlight for at least a few hours. The artificial intelligence leader debuted on the Nasdaq on Thursday. It initially saw its share price climb as high as $115, up more than 38% from the offering price, before giving back a large chunk of that. While it still ended the day with a 17% rise, seeing its fully diluted valuation soar past $2 trillion, the share price has fallen further in premarket trading on Friday.

While there are plenty of reasons to be optimistic about Anthropic, it is coming to market at a challenging moment for the AI narrative, and concerns about the sustainability of its business model remain.

AI jitters weren't helped on Friday after a report by Hunterbrook Media suggested chip giant AMD's ties with Chinese entities could attract greater US regulatory scrutiny. Hunterbrook is shorting the firm. An AMD spokesman said, "The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships."

All these tech worries hit Asian markets hard this week. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan tumbled 8.5%, the biggest weekly loss since March 2020.

This latest round of AI anxiety was supercharged last week by the dramatic ousting of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The erstwhile chief executive said on Monday that he “would be honored” to return to the company, a sentiment supported by many Silicon Valley leaders and even US President Donald Trump. However, the Nvidia board disagreed and said it has no plans to bring back the founder.

The longtime AI darling has shed an eye-popping $2 trillion in market cap in about six weeks, and the US Securities and Exchange Commission is now investigating the chipmaker, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Given this dramatic backdrop, Nvidia's earnings release on Tuesday seemed like a bit of a sideshow. The chipmaker beat revenue estimates for the 17th consecutive time, with third-quarter sales more than doubling to $115.84 billion. It also bumped up its fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to 75% year-on-year. However, interim CEO Colette Kress was obviously unable to answer the questions that really matter to investors, namely who will succeed Huang in the long term and what is happening with the external investigations.

Likely in response to the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration said on Monday that it would further limit China’s accessto advanced AI chips, including by restricting shipments via Southeast Asian countries that are often viewed as conduits to China. China’s Commerce Ministry said Beijing would take countermeasures if the ‌US ⁠imposed the new rule.

One might have expected this to make for some awkwardness when Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping alongside the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen on Thursday for a trilateral meeting that also included Russian President Vladimir Putin. While the Chinese and Russian leaders did pledge on Wednesday to stand up against trade "protectionism," clearly a dig at the US, the actual meeting mostly featured warm smiles and handshakes.

This supposedly “high-stakes” discussion didn’t produce any real breakthroughs. The three leaders put out a “peace declaration” on Thursday reaffirming that a nuclear war should never be fought, while also pledging to advance United Nations reforms, increase supplies of refined petroleum products, and uphold state officials’ immunity in international courts.

One party was noticeably absent from the meeting: Europe. Of course, the European Union isn’t part of APEC, but given the matters under discussion – including energy security, nuclear proliferation and the ongoing conflicts – it was noteworthy that Europe was left out. It’s another reminder of Europe’s inability to turn its economic heft into geopolitical power.

Nevertheless, the EU is reaching out to a trading partner closer to home this week. The UK and EU are holding a summit on Friday to focus on cooperation in trade, energy and mobility. This will be UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s first chance to show how serious he is about strengthening the relationship. He has previously stated that he would like to see Brexit reversed in his lifetime. He’s 56.

Heading back to the US, the drumbeat for Fed tightening picked up this week. Fed minutes from the October meeting showed that most policymakers believed additional interest rate hikes would be necessary to return inflation to the central bank’s 2% target, with some even considering a 50-basis-point rise.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller reinforced that on Wednesday, saying the Fed needed to get “aggressive” and shock people to ensure that today’s 3% inflation rate would not become entrenched. This came after St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem on Tuesday said “several” hikes would likely be needed.

Meanwhile, US October retail sales came in higher than expected, rising 0.2% after an unrevised 0.8% surge in September. Import prices also rose more than expected, reinforcing the hot inflation reports released last week, as elevated energy prices crept into other goods and services.

However, oil prices are on track for another weekly decline. Crude was pulled in opposite directions this week by expectations for a near-term glut and continued attacks in the Middle East. Brent crude (LCOc) was holding above $90 a barrel on Friday morning.
